claim: The effective reproductive number Re is a key indicator of the growth of an epidemic.
source: The effective reproductive number Re is a key indicator of the growth of an epidemic.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational concept.

claim: In early 2020, in the majority of countries the estimated Re dropped below 1 only after the introduction of major non-pharmaceutical interventions.
source: We show that, in early 2020, in the majority of countries the estimated Re dropped below 1 only after the introduction of major non-pharmaceutical interventions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data analysis in the results section.

claim: For Europe the implementation of non-pharmaceutical interventions was broadly associated with reductions in the estimated Re.
source: For Europe the implementation of non-pharmaceutical interventions was broadly associated with reductions in the estimated Re.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Relaxing non-pharmaceutical interventions had more varied effects on subsequent Re estimates globally.
source: Globally though, relaxing non-pharmaceutical interventions had more varied effects on subsequent Re estimates.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by analysis in Figure 5.

claim: The framework is used as the official source of Re estimates for SARS-CoV-2 in Switzerland.
source: Our framework is useful to inform governments and the general public on the status of epidemics in their country, and is used as the official source of Re estimates for SARS-CoV-2 in Switzerland.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual claim about the method's application.

claim: The effective reproductive number Re quantifies the average number of secondary infections caused by a primary infected individual.
source: It quantifies the average number of secondary infections caused by a primary infected individual.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the introduction, drawing on established epidemiological knowledge.

claim: Re has a natural threshold value of 1, below which the epidemic reduces in size.
source: It also has a natural threshold value of 1, below which the epidemic reduces in size Anderson and May, 1991; Nishiura and Chowell, 2009.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established epidemiological literature.

claim: Re typically changes during the course of an epidemic as a result of the depletion of susceptible individuals, changed contact behaviour, seasonality of the pathogen, or the effect of pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions.
source: Re typically changes during the course of an epidemic as a result of the depletion of susceptible individuals, changed contact behaviour, seasonality of the pathogen, or the effect of pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) (Anderson and May, 1991; Delamater et al., 2019; Scire et al., 2020; Ali et al., 2020; Flaxman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological literature.

claim: Infection incidence based methods rely on few, simple assumptions and are less prone to model misspecifications compared to compartmental models.
source: We focus on the latter class of methods as they rely on few, simple assumptions, are less prone to model misspecifications, and are well-suited for ongoing monitoring of the epidemic (Gostic et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for method choice, supported by citation.

claim: Infection events cannot be observed directly.
source: The infection incidence based methods face the difficulty that infection events cannot be observed directly (Gostic et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a fundamental challenge in epidemiology, supported by citation.

claim: It is important to relate Re estimates to the timing of infection events because this allows multiple proxies of infection events, with differing delays, to be used separately to monitor the same epidemic.
source: It is important to relate Re estimates to the timing of infection events because this allows multiple proxies of infection events, with differing delays, to be used separately to monitor the same epidemic (Scire et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological rationale supported by citation.

claim: If Re is placed properly on the infection timescale, it can be compared directly to external covariates like weather and interventions.
source: If Re is placed properly on this timescale, it can be compared directly to external covariates like weather and interventions (Flaxman et al., 2020; Soltesz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological advantage supported by citations.

claim: Depending on the method used to infer the timing of infections from the observed incidence time series, one can introduce biases such as smoothing sudden changes in Re.
source: However, depending on the method used to infer the timing of infections from the observed incidence time series, one can also introduce biases such as smoothing sudden changes in Re (Gostic et al., 2020; Goldstein et al., 2009; Petermann and Wyler, 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological challenge supported by citations.

claim: The method accurately estimates the effective reproductive number.
source: The results show that the method accurately estimates the effective reproductive number (Figure 1; metrics described in Materials and Methods).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Across most time points, the 95% confidence interval includes the true Re value.
source: Across most time points, the 95% confidence interval includes the true Re value (coverage; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results in Figure 1B.

claim: The low root mean squared error (RMSE) indicates that the point estimates closely track the true Re value.
source: The low root mean squared error (RMSE) indicates that our point estimates closely track the true Re value (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results in Figure 1C.

claim: The method correctly infers whether Re is significantly above or below 1 in the simulated scenario.
source: Importantly, we correctly infer whether Re is significantly above or below 1 in this scenario: we never infer that Re is significantly above 1 when the true value is below 1, and only for two time points the estimates are significantly below 1 for some simulations when the true value is a little above 1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results in Figure 1D.

claim: Due to the smoothing step prior to deconvolution, the method slightly misestimates Re during steep changes.
source: Due to the smoothing step prior to deconvolution, we slightly misestimate Re during steep changes (see Appendix 2, and Appendix 3—figure 1 for more scenarios).
evidence: This is a limitation identified through simulation analysis.

claim: The inclusion of smoothing greatly improves the performance across scenarios with different types of observation noise.
source: However, the inclusion of smoothing greatly improves the performance across scenarios with different types of observation noise (Appendix 3—figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results in Appendix 3.

claim: The block-bootstrapping method greatly improves coverage compared to the out-of-the-box EpiEstim method.
source: Our block-bootstrapping method greatly improves coverage compared to the out-of-the-box EpiEstim method.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological improvement based on simulation results.

claim: The method outperforms the common approach of using a fixed delay to infer the infection incidence time series.
source: Our method also outperforms the common approach of using a fixed delay to infer the infection incidence time series (Appendix 3—figure 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparative simulation results.

claim: Misspecifying the mean of the delay distribution between infection and case observation by up to 2 days does not have a strong effect on the Re estimates.
source: Misspecifying the mean of the delay distribution between infection and case observation by up to 2 days does not have a strong effect on the Re estimates, whereas larger misspecifications by 5 or 10 days lead to a more substantial decrease in coverage (Appendix 3—figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sensitivity analysis in simulations.

claim: Allowing for time-varying delay distributions has a pronounced effect on the estimated Re only when changes in the mean of the delay distribution are large.
source: Correspondingly, allowing for time-varying delay distributions has a pronounced effect on the estimated Re only when changes in the mean of the delay distribution are large (Appendix 3—figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation analysis.

claim: The most recent Re estimate lies further in the past than the most recent observed incidence data due to the delay between infection and case observation.
source: The most recent Re estimate lies further in the past than the most recent observed incidence data due to the delay between infection and case observation.
evidence: This is a methodological characteristic of the approach.

claim: The difference in confidence interval performance is particularly striking during periods of high case incidence when the EpiEstim uncertainty interval is very narrow.
source: This difference is particularly striking during periods of high case incidence (e.g. October 2020), when the EpiEstim uncertainty interval is very narrow.
evidence: This is observed in the stability analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The last few Re estimates can lay outside of the stabilized confidence interval, in particular when the real Re trend is increasing.
source: This analysis shows that the last few Re estimates can lay outside of the stabilized confidence interval, in particular when the real Re trend is increasing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation analysis in Appendix 4.

claim: There is a trade-off between timeliness and accuracy when publishing Re estimates.
source: This highlights a trade-off between timeliness and accuracy when publishing Re estimates.
evidence: This is inferred from the stability analysis results.

claim: For each of the three types of case report in Switzerland, the authors estimate the time-varying empirical delay distribution for the delay from infection to reporting.
source: For each of these three types of case report, we estimate the time-varying empirical delay distribution for the delay from infection to reporting.
evidence: This is a methodological approach described for Swiss data analysis.

claim: Using FOPH data on the fraction of cases infected abroad, the authors can correct the Re estimate for imported cases.
source: Using FOPH data on the fraction of cases infected abroad, we can correct our Re estimate for imported cases.
evidence: This is a methodological approach described for Swiss data analysis.

claim: The estimated Re value corrected for imports is a lower bound for the Re estimate which would be obtained if the authors could account for the location of infection of all cases detected in Switzerland or exported out of the country.
source: Thus, the estimated Re value corrected for imports is a lower bound for the Re estimate which would be obtained if we could account for the location of infection of all cases detected in Switzerland or exported out of the country.
evidence: This is a limitation stated based on methodological reasoning.

claim: The estimates from EpiNow2 and the authors' method follow a qualitatively similar trend.
source: The estimates from EpiNow2 and ours follow a qualitatively similar trend, although the EpiNow2 estimates are smoother and there is a small lag between both estimates, likely due to differences in the specified observation delay distribution.
evidence: This is observed in the comparison shown in Figure 3.

claim: The authors' method is the only one that can account for variations through time in delay distributions and combine symptom onset data with case data.
source: To the best of our knowledge, our method is the only one that can account for variations through time in delay distributions and combine symptom onset data with case data.
evidence: This is stated as a unique feature of the method based on comparison with other methods.

claim: The authors developed an online dashboard presenting daily-updated results of the Re estimation method applied to COVID-19 case data from 170 countries.
source: We developed an online dashboard (https://ibz-shiny.ethz.ch/covid-19-re-international/) on which we present daily-updated results of this Re estimation method applied to COVID-19 case data from 170 countries (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the implementation of the method.

claim: For most countries, the authors include multiple observation sources, such as daily incidence of COVID-19 cases and deaths, and, when available, hospital admissions.
source: For most countries, we include multiple observation sources, such as daily incidence of COVID-19 cases and deaths, and, when available, hospital admissions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data used in the method.

claim: Of the 20 investigated European countries, all except Sweden implemented a lockdown in spring 2020.
source: Of the countries investigated, all except Sweden implemented a lockdown (19/20).
evidence: This is a factual statement based on data collection from news reports.

claim: Using case data, Re was inferred to be significantly above one prior to the lockdown measures in nearly all countries with a lockdown (15/19).
source: Using case data, we inferred that Re was significantly above one prior to the lockdown measures in nearly all countries with a lockdown (15/19; Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of European data shown in Table 1.

claim: Denmark and Germany had an estimated Re significantly below one prior to the lockdown date.
source: Denmark, which had a complex outbreak consisting of two initial waves, and Germany, which experienced a cluster of early cases, had an estimated Re significantly below one prior to this date.
evidence: This is stated as an exception to the general finding, based on data analysis.

claim: For countries with very short delays between the lockdown and the estimated date that Re<1, the authors cannot exclude the possibility that the 'true' Re may have been below 1 prior to the lockdown since the pipeline introduces smoothing to the estimates.
source: For countries with very short delays between the lockdown and the estimated date that Re<1 (e.g. Austria, Switzerland) we can not exclude the possibility that the 'true' Re may have been below 1 prior to the lockdown since our pipeline introduces smoothing to the estimates (see Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a caveat stated based on methodological limitations.

claim: In Europe, large increases in stringency are associated with larger decreases in Re 7–14 days after the change in stringency index.
source: In Europe we also see that large increases in stringency are associated with larger decreases in Re 7–14 days after the change in SI.
evidence: This is observed in the analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The association between decreases in stringency and changes in Re is heterogeneous on all continents.
source: However, the association between decreases in stringency and changes in Re is heterogeneous on all continents (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in the analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Reversing non-pharmaceutical interventions had a different effect than introducing them.
source: This suggests that reversing non-pharmaceutical interventions had a different effect than introducing them.
evidence: This is inferred from the heterogeneous association observed in Figure 5.

claim: In Europe, increased mobility in residential areas, and decreased mobility at workplaces or grocery stores is associated with decreases in Re.
source: Increased mobility in residential areas, and decreased mobility at workplaces or grocery stores is associated with decreases in Re.
evidence: This is observed in the analysis shown in Figure 5B for Europe.

claim: The inferred Re curve can be over-smoothed on simulated data, but this disadvantage is outweighed by the increased stability of the estimates.
source: We showed that the inferred Re curve can be over-smoothed on simulated data, but that this disadvantage is outweighed by the increased stability of the estimates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from simulation analysis.

claim: The relative error in the Re estimates is small.
source: Overall, we show that the relative error in the Re estimates is small.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from simulation analysis.

claim: A unique advantage of the monitoring method is the parallel use of different types of observation data, all reflecting the same underlying infection process.
source: A unique advantage of the monitoring method we have developed is the parallel use of different types of observation data, all reflecting the same underlying infection process (Scire et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage, supported by citation.

claim: Comparing estimates from several types of data is a powerful way to evaluate the sensitivity of the results to the type of observations they were derived from.
source: Comparing estimates from several types of data is a powerful way to evaluate the sensitivity of the results to the type of observations they were derived from.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage.

claim: The method is applicable to any other type of incidence data, such as admissions to intensive care units or excess death data.
source: More generally, the method is applicable to any other type of incidence data, such as admissions to intensive care units or excess death data.
evidence: This is stated as a general applicability of the method.

claim: The authors have extended this method to make use of daily measurements of SARS-CoV-2 viral concentrations in wastewater.
source: We have also extended this method to make use of daily measurements of SARS-CoV-2 viral concentrations in wastewater (Huisman et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as an extension of the method, supported by citation.

claim: For 15 out of 20 European countries, the estimated Re was significantly above 1 prior to the lockdown in spring of 2020.
source: We showed that this argumentation cannot be applied universally: for 15 out of 20 European countries, we found that the estimated Re was significantly above 1 prior to the lockdown in spring of 2020.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of European data.

claim: Differences between continents in the association between changes in the stringency of NPIs and changes in Re could reflect differences in the speed with which lockdowns were put into practice, the de facto lockdown stringency, or socio-cultural aspects.
source: This could reflect differences in the speed with which lockdowns were put into practice (Kohanovski et al., 2022), the de facto lockdown stringency, or socio-cultural aspects (Sebhatu et al., 2020; Mbow et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for observed differences, supported by citations.

claim: Many African countries had early and strict government responses, often prior to the first detected cases, which are thought to have delayed the virus in establishing a foothold on the continent.
source: Many African countries had early and strict government responses, often prior to the first detected cases. These are thought to have delayed the virus in establishing a foothold on the continent (Mbow et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation, supported by citation.

claim: The analysis suggests that reversing non-pharmaceutical interventions may have a very different effect than introducing them.
source: Importantly, our analysis suggests that reversing non-pharmaceutical interventions may have a very different effect than introducing them.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: The difference in effect between implementing and lifting NPIs could be because the situation is not fully reverted: due to increased public awareness, testing, contact tracing, and quarantine measures still in place.
source: This could be because the situation is not fully reverted: due to increased public awareness, testing, contact tracing, and quarantine measures still in place.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for observed differences.

claim: There is increasing evidence that weather may be a factor influencing Re through its effect on people's behaviour and on properties of the virus.
source: In addition, there is increasing evidence that weather may be a factor influencing Re through its effect on people's behaviour and on properties of the virus (Morris et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as emerging evidence, supported by citation.

claim: The authors use local polynomial regression (LOESS) with 1st order polynomials and tricubic weights to smooth the observed incidence data prior to deconvolution.
source: To smooth the incidence data, we use local polynomial regression (LOESS) with 1st order polynomials and tricubic weights.
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the pipeline.

claim: The smoothing parameter alpha is set such that 21 days of data are included in the local neighbourhood of each point.
source: The smoothing parameter alpha is set such that we include 21 days of data in the local neighbourhood of each point.
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the pipeline.

claim: The authors extended the deconvolution method of Goldstein et al., 2009 to deal with zero-incidence case observations and time-varying delay distributions.
source: To this end, we extended the deconvolution method of Goldstein et al., 2009, which is itself an adaptation of the Richardson-Lucy algorithm (Richardson, 1972; Lucy, 1974) (essentially an expectation maximisation algorithm), to deal with zero-incidence case observations and time-varying delay distributions.
evidence: This is a methodological contribution described in the methods section.

claim: The authors use the EpiEstim method to estimate Re from a time series of infection incidence.
source: Once we have obtained an estimate for the time series of infection incidence, we use the method developed by Cori et al., 2013, implemented in the EpiEstim R package, to estimate Re.
evidence: This is a methodological detail, supported by citation.

claim: For the gradually-changing Re estimates, Re is assumed to be constant over a sliding window of 3 days.
source: For the gradually-changing Re estimates, we assume Re is constant over a sliding window of 3 days (τ=3 in EpiEstim), i.e. the reported Re estimate for day T summarises the average Re over a 3 day period ending on day T.
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the estimation approach.

claim: The authors use the mean of the posterior distribution of Re as the point estimate.
source: In both cases, we use the mean of the posterior distribution of Re as the point estimate.
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the estimation approach.

claim: The authors construct 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for Re to account for the uncertainty in the case observations.
source: To account for the uncertainty in the case observations, we construct 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for Re.
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the uncertainty quantification.

claim: The authors use an overlapping block bootstrap because the empirical residuals of most countries are autocorrelated.
source: Since the empirical residuals of most countries are autocorrelated (see Appendix 5—figure 2), we use an overlapping block bootstrap.
evidence: This is a methodological choice justified by data characteristics.

claim: The authors use a block size of 10 for the block bootstrap method because it tended to work well in various simulation settings.
source: We tried different sizes and found that b=10 tended to work well in various simulation settings (Appendix 5—figure 6).
evidence: This is a methodological choice based on simulation results.

claim: The final reported interval is the union of the credible interval and the 95% bootstrap confidence interval.
source: The final reported interval is then the union of the credible interval and the 95% bootstrap confidence interval.
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the uncertainty quantification.

claim: The authors parametrise the discretised infectivity profile using COVID-19 serial interval estimates from Nishiura et al., 2020.
source: We parametrise the discretised infectivity profile ws using COVID-19 serial interval estimates from the literature (Nishiura et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological detail, supported by citation.

claim: The incubation period is parametrised by a gamma distribution with mean 5.3 days and SD 3.2 days.
source: The incubation period is parametrised by a gamma distribution with mean 5.3 days and SD 3.2 days (Linton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological detail, supported by citation.

claim: For countries without access to line list data, delays from symptom onset to observation are assumed to be gamma-distributed, with parameters taken from the literature.
source: For countries for which we do not have access to line list data, i.e. all except Switzerland, Germany and Hong Kong at the time of writing, we assume delays from symptom onset to observation to be gamma-distributed, with parameters taken from the literature.
evidence: This is a methodological detail, with parameters from literature.

claim: For Switzerland, Germany and Hong Kong, the authors use line lists to build time-varying empirical distributions on delays between symptom onset and case confirmation, hospitalisation or death.
source: For Switzerland, Germany and Hong Kong, we use line lists to build time-varying empirical distributions on delays between symptom onset and case confirmation, hospitalisation or death.
evidence: This is a methodological detail for specific countries.

claim: The infection incidence is simulated forward in time from a Poisson distribution, corresponding to equation (6), using the specified Re time series and the discretised serial interval for SARS-CoV-2.
source: The infection incidence on day t is drawn from a Poisson distribution, corresponding to equation (6), using the specified Re time series and the discretised serial interval for SARS-CoV-2 (Nishiura et al., 2020) as the infectivity profile (see Cori et al., 2013; Web Appendix 11).
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the simulation approach, supported by citations.

claim: Daily updated results of the method on global COVID-19 data are available online at https://ibz-shiny.ethz.ch/covid-19-re-international/.
source: Daily updated results of our method on global COVID-19 data are available online on https://ibz-shiny.ethz.ch/covid-19-re-international/.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the availability of results.

claim: The source code of the software pipeline is openly accessible at https://github.com/covid-19-Re/shiny-dailyRe.
source: The source code of the software pipeline is openly accessible at https://github.com/covid-19-Re/shiny-dailyRe; Angst, 2022
evidence: This is a factual statement about code availability.

claim: The code necessary to reproduce the figures and analyses presented in this paper is available at https://github.com/covid-19-Re/paper-code.
source: the code necessary to reproduce the figures and analyses presented in this paper is available at https://github.com/covid-19-Re/paper-code; Huisman, 2022.
evidence: This is a factual statement about code availability.
